neutral_facts.value: The accused, who was the husband of the deceased, was alleged to have harassed the deceased due to insufficient dowry. The deceased was admitted to a hospital with severe burns, and a dying declaration was recorded by an Executive Magistrate. The declaration stated that the accused had poured kerosene on her and set her on fire. The deceased's relatives applied for the recording of the statement, and the magistrate recorded it after examining the deceased's fitness. The prosecution relied on the dying declaration and the testimony of the deceased's relatives and a village Sarpanch to establish harassment due to dowry demands. However, the evidence was questioned for its reliability and voluntariness, and the deceased's short temper and the absence of the accused on the day of the incident were noted. The High Court disbelieved the dying declaration in part, and the Supreme Court found that the prosecution failed to prove harassment beyond reasonable doubt.

quotes.text: The learned trial court convicted all the three accused persons for the offence punishable under Section 304-B of IPC for causing the dowry death of the deceased and accordingly sentenced them to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of seven years along with fine.

The High Court, by the impugned judgment, while observing that the appeal preferred by Dhan Kaur, mother-in-law of the deceased stood abated as she had died during the proceedings; dismissed the appeals filed by the State of Haryana and Pavitar Singh (PW-3), and partly allowed the appeals filed by Jora Singh, father-in-law of the deceased and the appellant herein thereby acquitting Jora Singh, father-in-law of the charge levelled against him under Section 304-B of IPC, but confirmed the conviction and sentence awarded by the learned trial court to the appellant herein.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the appellant harassed the deceased on account of insufficiency of dowry, leading to her death by burning. They relied on the dying declaration of the deceased and the evidence of relatives and witnesses to establish the case under Section 304-B of the IPC.

quotes.text: It is the prosecution case that the appellant used to harass the deceased on account of insufficiency of dowry.
The prosecution relies on the evidence of Pavitar Singh (PW-3), brother of the deceased, Randhir Singh (PW-4), father of the deceased and Major Singh (PW-6), Sarpanch of the village.

defence_argument.value: The defence argued that the dying declaration was not reliable and was tutored by the deceased's relatives. They also contended that there was no evidence to prove harassment on account of non-fulfillment of dowry, and the case under Section 304-B of the IPC was not made out.

quotes.text: He submits that the very first information given by the deceased herself to the doctor while admitting to the hospital, would show that the deceased had put up kerosene on herself and set herself on fire.
He submits that the said dying declaration was a tutored one at the instance of her relatives and the conviction solely based on the same is not sustainable.

legal_principle_applied.value: The Supreme Court applied the principle that a conviction based on a dying declaration must be supported by evidence that the declaration is trustworthy, reliable, and free from doubt.

quotes.text: No doubt, that a conviction can be solely recorded on the basis of dying declaration. However, for doing so, the court must come to a conclusion that the dying declaration is trustworthy, reliable and one which inspires confidence.
In the totality of the circumstances, it cannot be said that the dying declaration (Ex. P.L.) is free from doubt.
